theme.name: EU Directive conflicts with GB exemption
theme.claim: The new Directive 2014/45/EU replaces the pre-1960 exemption with conditions (at least 30 years old, out of production, not substantially changed), so GB law must be amended if historic vehicles are to stay exempt.

text.line: A new European Roadworthiness Directive makes changes to the existing vehicle testing scheme, including the provisions for exempting vehicles of historical interest.

The Directive still enables exemptions from regular testing, and in respect of vehicles of historical interest, it applies to vehicles manufactured or registered for the first time at least 30 years ago, which are no longer in production and have not been substantially changed.
The Directive sets new rules on periodic roadworthiness testing for vehicles and their trailers and repeals the old EU Directive 2009/40/EC.

In Great Britain all vehicles manufactured before 1960 are exempt from regular road-worthiness testing.
EU Directive 2014/45 changes the rules around this.

The new rules allow Member States to exempt vehicles of historical interest (VHIs) from testing if they are at least 30 years old, no longer in production and have not had substantial changes made to them.
If we wish to continue to exempt VHIs from regular testing to implement the new EU requirements we’ll need to update GB law.
The new Directive also allows Member States to determine the periodicity of testing for VHIs if not exempt.
New EU Directive 2014/45 (“the Directive”) sets out minimum requirements for periodic road-worthiness testing of vehicles used on public roads.
Under current GB and EU law all vehicles that were manufactured or registered before 1960 can be exempted from periodic testing.
The new EU directive still enables exemptions from regular testing, but vehicles must be at least 30 years old, no longer in production and should not be substantially changed.
If we wish to continue to exempt VHIs we will need to implement EU requirements and amend GB law.
2) Rationale for intervention At the moment GB legislation simply allows all vehicles manufactured before 1960 to be exempt from roadworthiness testing.
The ‘substantial change’ provision in the Directive means we will need to amend GB legislation to implement the requirements of the Directive, to continue to exempt VHIs from MOT testing.

theme.name: Road safety risk of older vehicles
theme.claim: Older vehicles often lack safety features and need to be safe and well maintained, so any exemption from testing carries a road safety risk that must be managed.

text.line: It is also important that these vehicles are safe and appropriately maintained, especially as many older vehicles lack appropriate safety features, to ensure the risk to road safety is reduced.

theme.name: Exemption only for genuinely original vehicles
theme.claim: The 'not substantially changed' requirement is a useful safeguard ensuring that exempted vehicles are in the original condition they purport to be and that people cannot profit from exemption on altered vehicles.

text.line: This ensures that the vehicles benefiting from MOT exemptions are actually in the original condition they purport to be.
This is a useful amendment which aims to ensure that people who drive vehicles which have been significantly changed cannot profit from an exemption.
